strengths: QuEST addresses an important compression problem through a coherent combination of timestep-dependent activation quantization, selective weight finetuning, and supervision from a full-precision teacher. The sensitivity analysis provides useful empirical motivation for targeting time embeddings and attention layers. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b05/review-experiment-geb6ee6k/call-a7823c9b8f06493d91f3684b752cbf9d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The improvements over the evaluated PTQ baselines are substantial. Table 3 reports W4A4 FIDs of 5.64 on LSUN-Bedrooms and 11.76 on LSUN-Churches where the baselines fail. Figure 4 also demonstrates coherent bedroom images under W4A4.

Evaluation covers four models across unconditional, class-conditional, and text-to-image generation, generally using 50,000 images for LDM evaluation and 10,000 COCO prompts for Stable Diffusion. The datasets, pretrained models, and principal comparison methods are referenced.

The component ablations support the method's practical value: Table 6 improves FID from 12.56 with TAQuant to 6.41 after time-embedding alignment and 5.78 after attention alignment. Quantization time decreases from 23.08 to 15.25 GPU-hours relative to Q-Diffusion with the same calibration-set size.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is not sound as written. For the stated MSE loss on final activations in Section 3.3.1, the second-order Taylor expansion is exact regardless of perturbation magnitude, so large perturbations do not establish Proposition 3.1's claimed breakdown. Theorem 3.2 also provides no proof that a shared set of quantized weights, particularly the selected subset, can fit the perturbed activations. The empirical gains remain meaningful, but the claimed sufficiency guarantee is unsupported.

The most relevant comparison is missing: Efficient-DM is explicitly discussed as efficient quantization-aware finetuning but is excluded from the experiments. Consequently, comparisons primarily against PTQ methods do not establish the proposed approach's advantage over existing efficient finetuning. Matched quality–cost comparisons and an equal-parameter alternative layer-selection baseline would better establish the contribution.

The central Stable Diffusion W4A4 claim is inadequately evaluated. Table 5 reports only CLIP score, which measures text–image alignment and cannot establish perceptual quality; Figure 4 contains only bedroom examples. Moreover, ImageNet W4A4 Inception Score drops from 364.73 to 202.45 despite improved FID. These results warrant complementary quality evaluation and closer analysis of the remaining degradation.

Important implementation details are missing, including quantizer granularity and initialization, gradients through rounding, exact selected layers for each model, and Stable Diffusion calibration prompts. The staged optimization schedule and precise operator coverage of 'full W4A4' also need clarification for reproducibility.

Practical inference benefits remain unverified: the paper reports model sizes and quantization costs without measurements of actual low-bit inference latency or peak inference memory. Table 6 establishes faster quantization while using approximately 20% more memory than the PTQ baseline, so it does not demonstrate a general improvement in both time and memory.
